 East Texans prepare to fall back for daylight saving time during Halloween weekend 
 East Texans prepare to fall back for daylight saving time during Halloween weekend By April Pierdant Published : Oct. 27, 2026 at 10:33 PM CDT | Updated : 6 hours ago Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google TYLER, Texas (KLTV) - From trick-or-treat to turn-back-the-clock — East Texans are gearing up for a Halloween weekend full of festivities, plus an extra hour of sleep Sunday morning as daylight saving time ends. But experts say gaining an hour still takes adjustment for our bodies.
 For Tyler mom Gracie Chapman, Halloween is family tradition.
 “We definitely trick or treat,” Chapman said.
 She says it’s also a chance to be with their community.
 “We’ll go around our neighborhood. It gets pretty crazy,” Chapman said.
 But with daylight saving time ending the day after Halloween, Chapman says it might get a little bit more crazy with her kids.
 “I know for us, we’re usually ready for them to wake up right at seven, so it’d be nice if they sleep in a little further, but we’ll see if they actually do that,” Chapman said.
 As clocks fall back Sunday, gaining an hour of sleep, Dr. Raghavendra Ghuge with the Sleep Medicine Institute of Texas in Tyler says it can be hard to adjust at the beginning.
 “One hour might seem not that bad, but the entire biological clock has to shift a whole hour. And that’s quite difficult,” Ghuge said.
 Ghuge says that one hour does more work for your body than you might think.
 “If you can think about light as a steering wheel of your biological clock, exposure to light controls your wake time, sleep time, alertness, sleepiness, bodily functions, liver physiology, brain physiology,” Ghuge said. “So a lot of stuff gets done in the brain in that one hour that you’re sleeping or not sleeping.”
 19-year-old Alexandria Brown says she plans to spend the weekend with friends — and doesn’t think the time change will affect her as much.
 “This weekend wouldn’t affect me, but it’s more or less like continuing after that because I do drive an hour for school,” Brown said.
 Dr. Ghuge recommends easing in by 15 to 20 minutes a day ahead of the change during bedtime, getting early morning sunlight, and watching late caffeine.
 Daylight saving time is currently observed in 48 states. A proposed federal change — known as the ‘Sunshine Protection Act’ — would end the twice-a-year clock switch, while still allowing states to opt out. Right now, that bill is still pending in the Senate, and no vote is scheduled on it.
